title: Widespread naturally variable human exons aid genetic interpretation

paper_content.abstract: Most mammalian genes undergo alternative splicing. The splicing of some exons has been acquired or lost in specific mammalian lineages, but differences in splicing within the human population are poorly understood. Using GTEx tissue transcriptomes from 838 individuals, we identified 57,271 “naturally variable exons” (NVEs) – exons which are included in mRNAs in some individuals but entirely excluded from others (or vice versa). NVEs impact three quarters of protein-coding genes, occur at all population frequencies, and are often absent from reference annotations. NVEs are more abundant in genes depleted of genetic loss-of-function mutations and aid in the interpretation of causal genetic variants. Genetic variants modulate the splicing of many NVEs, and 5’ untranslated region and coding-region NVEs are often associated with increased and decreased gene expression, respectively. Together, our findings characterize abundant splicing variation in the human population, with implications for a range of human genetic analyses.
paper_content.introduction:
Nearly all human genes undergo alternative splicing, in which distinct mRNAs derived from different combinations of exons and splice sites are produced from the same gene1. Small changes in mRNA sequence can exert large effects, including the addition/deletion of protein domains2,3, or production of functional versus nonfunctional isoforms, and dysregulation of splicing contributes to human disease4,5. Understanding variation in alternative splicing is therefore important in understanding physiological and disease mechanisms.

Evolutionarily conserved alternative exons tend to preserve protein reading frame6, and often exhibit tissue-specific regulation7. In addition, comparison across mammalian species has identified thousands of cases of complete loss or gain of the splicing of exons8, with more recently evolved exons more likely to occur in 5’ UTRs, where they are often associated with increased gene expression8. Gain or loss of the splicing of an exon in the coding sequence (CDS) may also influence expression by changing the reading frame, often triggering nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD)9,10. However, the evolution of alternative splicing within the human species remains poorly understood.

Most alternative exons are generally assumed to be spliced in all individuals, perhaps with different inclusion levels, a pattern which we call ‘canonical’ alternative splicing. Some such splicing differences are driven by genetic variation. Large-scale genetic association studies have associated changes in the usage of many alternatively spliced exons with single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), designated splicing quantitative trait loci (sQTLs)11,12. However, these variants typically have modest effect sizes, and their molecular mechanisms are often unclear. Ultra-rare genetic variants can sometimes lead to inclusion of previously unseen, “cryptic” exons or splice sites13. Some recent studies suggest that many exons are missing from transcriptome reference annotations, occurring only in a subset of transcriptomic datasets11,14,15. The availability of tissue transcriptomes from nearly 1000 individuals in the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project presents an opportunity to characterize human variation at the exon level, asking how often the presence/absence of individual exons or splice sites varies between the transcriptomes of different individuals.

One key challenge in the study of unannotated transcripts is assessing which reflect technical artifacts or other types of noise16,17, which are reproducible, and which have phenotypic effects18. A cross-species analysis has suggested that many unannotated splicing events in longer-lived organisms may represent “transcript drift”, and are often nonfunctional until they begin to splice in at higher levels19. However, another recent study found that lowly used exons that trigger NMD broadly impact gene expression in human lymphoblastoid cell lines, and can help interpret complex trait loci10.

Here, we define “naturally variable exons” (NVEs) as exons whose splicing is variable within the human population (i.e., not present in every individual), focusing on alternative “skipped” or “cassette” exons, and alternative splice sites, which extend or truncate exons. We introduce a statistical approach that estimates the population frequency with which NVEs are meaningfully included (at levels above 5%) in a human cohort, generating a quantitative atlas of splicing variation across tissues. Using data from GTEx, we find that NVEs impact most human genes, are sometimes associated with changes in gene expression, and can aid in the interpretation of non-coding genetic variants.
paper_content.results:
Generating a catalog of human NVEs
In order to generate a catalog of high-quality NVEs, we obtained mapped RNA-seq reads from 14,000 GTEx samples representing 49 tissues from 838 individuals11. To perform quality control and ensure accurate estimates of NVEs in the dataset, we devised a straightforward Bayesian approach. The method de-noises estimates by sharing signals across samples and enables estimation of the uncertainty in exon usage of each NVE.

To illustrate the method, consider an NVE of the alternative splice site variety, used in some individuals as an alternative to a canonical or “cognate” splice site, used in all people. The proportional use of the NVE within an individual – the “percent spliced in” (PSI or Ψ) – can be estimated from the proportion of RNA-seq reads that span the NVE and cognate exon junctions (EJs) (Supplementary Fig. 1A)20. NVEs tend to have fewer total junction reads per sample, making some estimates of Ψ less certain (Supplementary Fig. 1B). We therefore de-noised these estimates using a beta-binomial model, employing a mixture of 3 beta distributions for reasons discussed below. The workflow is described in Supplementary Fig. 1C, Methods and Supplementary Note Sections A-D. The method fits a smooth function representing the NVE’s underlying Ψ distribution across the population from the observed splice junction reads for an NVE across individuals in a tissue. We chose a mixture of 3 betas model because of its flexibility to model many different distributions and because many NVEs are associated with sQTLs (see below), which have 3 possible genotypes that may each generate distinct levels of splicing. The mixture of betas model can be used to assess uncertainty in Ψ values, and to estimate the proportion of individuals that splice the NVE at any given level. Here, we defined NVEs as alternative exons or splice sites that have estimated Ψ values of at least 5% in between 1% and 99% of the population in a particular tissue (see “Methods”); exons with Ψ ≥ 5% in over 99% of individuals are considered canonical alternative exons, and exons that don’t meet either of these criteria may be considered rare or cryptic exons. Using this definition, we identified 414,141 NVE-tissue pairs across all 49 tissues in the GTEx dataset (Supplementary Data 1), representing 57,271 unique NVEs. Like canonical alternative exons, NVEs are roughly balanced between the alternative splice site and skipped exon types (Supplementary Data 2).

Using these data, we define an interpretable summary statistic, exon frequency (EF), that describes the frequency of splicing of an NVE in a population, somewhat analogous to allele frequency (AF). The EF of an NVE in a tissue is the estimated proportion of individuals that splice the NVE at a threshold Ψ level or above. We typically employ a 5% Ψ threshold here because previous studies have suggested that this level of inclusion is near the lowest level where sequence conservation is commonly observed19. Distributions of EF values using different Ψ cutoffs are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1D
paper_content.methods:
Ethics statement
No primary data were generated for this study. Person-related data were obtained through authorized access from primary data controllers.

Datasets
GTEx release v8. From the GTEx download data portal, we downloaded splicing “phenotype” files, which were originally used as inputs of the original sQTL study in GTEx (v8 phg38). We accessed it using the GTEx data browser, and you can also use the requester pay google cloud bucket (gs://gtex-resources/GTEx_Analysis_v8_QTLs). Protected data, such as genotypes and metadata, were accessed via dbGaP (study accession: phs000424.v8.p2).

GTEx fine-mapped sQTLs and eQTLs. Baberia et al. fine-mapped sQTLs and eQTLS in GTEx using the DAP-G fine-mapping method. We accessed this dataset using their Zenodo link. Note that fine-mapping was performed only on European ancestry samples from GTEx.

gnomAD. We accessed LOEUF scores from gnomAD v4.0 using the gnomAD data browser (linked here), which computed the LOEUF across nearly all genes in the genome.

GENCODE exon annotations. We accessed comprehensive transcript annotations from GENCODE v44 using their data browser, for use as our reference set of exons.

SpliceAI scores. SpliceAI scores have been computed across the genome (all possible SNP mutations). To compare the differences in SMS and spliceAI scores, we used a dataset that released all variants with SpliceAI scores above a nominal threshold (>0.1), which are available in the Illumina data browser (link: https://basespace.illumina.com/s/otSPW8hnhaZR). All other variants were set to 0.

Fine-mapped BioBank (GWAS) data
UKBB (96 traits): https://github.com/mkanai/finemapping-insights, including ASGR1 exon 4
Biobank Japan: https://pheweb.jp/downloads
FinnGen: https://www.finngen.fi/en/researchers/data_available

Data preprocessing
GTEx LeafCutter phenotypes. LeafCutter intron clusters were required to include only 2 or 3 introns, so we could classify them as alternative 3’ or 5’ splice sites or skipped exons, respectively. We mapped to genes and strands by scoring every splice site in the cluster, and picking the strand that had MaxEnt scores > 0 for all splice sites, excluding any clusters that did not score above zero across all splice sites on either strand as potential artefacts. Only protein-coding genes were included. Lastly, exons were required to be ≤ 500 bp in length and alternative splice sites were required to be within 500 bp of each other.

Generating estimates of Ψ values of NVEs
Many NVEs have fairly low inclusion levels, so to estimate their usage accurately, we built a model to assess their abundance in an RNA-sequencing sample. We considered a potential NVE in relation to a more frequently observed “cognate” junction in transcripts from the same gene.

PSI (Ψ) estimates the fraction of a gene’s transcripts that contain the exon or splice site of interest and is a widely used statistic to quantify splicing. It can be estimated from any RNA-seq dataset with sufficient read coverage of the alternative region:

ψ NVE = EJ reads NVE / (EJ reads NVE + EJ reads cognate)

We consider the exon or splice junction with fewer reads across all individuals a candidate NVE, and the exon or splice junction with more reads as the cognate.

Conditional on Ψ, the number of NVE reads in an RNA-seq dataset can be modeled as a binomial distribution, as defined by LeafCutter splicing33 clusters:

NVE reads | ψ ~ Binomial(EJ reads NVE + EJ reads cognate, Ψ NVE)

Note that we have to frame the exon junction reads slightly differently in alternative splice sites as compared to skipped exons to model the NVE (Supp. Fig. 1A).

Mixture of Betas binomial model
Partial pooling involves using information across samples to estimate effect sizes of individual samples by fitting a population distribution to the observed data and letting that inform effect size estimates for individuals54,55.

For proof of concept, the NVE population distribution can be modeled with a single beta distribution with parameters α and β:

ψ NVE ~ Beta(α, β)

Where α can be described as the pseudocount on the splicing of the NVEs splicing event, and β can be described as the pseudocount on the splicing of the cognate splicing event, respectively. In other words, in the absence of read count data, α and β provide an initial estimate of the splicing of the NVE.

A single beta distribution can capture several common situations (but not all – see Supplementary Note). One example of a distribution that a single beta cannot handle is a trimodal distribution, which would be expected for an NVE whose splicing differs between three subsets of the population. Because trimodal distributions are interesting biologically, potentially representing cases where a single variant (that may be absent or present in heterozygous or homozygous form) drives the inclusion of an NVE, we decided to fit a three-component mixture of betas model to all exons in the dataset. We compare this result to a single beta model in the Supplementary Note Sections E-F, and find that the summary statistic, EF, is fairly robust in both three- and one-component models.

For a three-component beta distribution, with parameters α and β, the NVE population distribution can be modeled with nine parameters:

ψ NVE ~ Σ i=1 to 3 γ i Beta(α i, β i)

Where γ i are weights that represent the fraction of the distribution coming from each individual beta distribution, requiring that all γ i ≥ 0, and that they sum to 1. Note that the triple-beta distribution can model a two-beta or single beta distribution by setting one or two of the γ parameters to zero. We can then estimate the population distribution of a given tissue sample:

PDF NVE = Σ i=1 to 3 γ i * PDF Beta(α i, β i)

The task is to predict the population distribution of a splicing event in a given tissue sample. We employ maximum likelihood estimation with the expectation maximization algorithm. The algorithm is initialized with uniform weights, α=(1,2,3), and β=(3,2,1) as an unbiased starting point able to capture symmetric and asymmetric distributions. It then iteratively performs the E-step to analytically find optimal weights γ, and the M-step to determine the α, β using the L-BFGS-B optimization algorithm. The method is represented graphically in Fig. 1A.

Alternative splice site NVEs
We searched for the optimal α, β, and γ parameters that best fit the data, using the expectation maximization framework (see Supplementary Note Sections B-C).

Skipped exon NVEs
Skipped exons are represented by three intron clusters: two introns supporting the inclusion of the exon, and one longer intron excluding the exon. We include events where both inclusion introns have numbers of reads that are not drastically different (see Supplementary Fig. 11), keeping one of the two inclusion introns to simplify the analysis. We then followed the same approach as for alternative splice sites to find the optimal parameters.

Calculation of exon frequency (EF) at a given Ψ threshold
We estimated the Ψ of all NVEs of length ≤ 500 (for skipped exons) or inter-splice site distance ≤ 500 bp (see Supp. Fig. 16), as this size capture the vast majority (>99%) of known internal exons and alternative splice sites in the human transcriptome. After obtaining the population parameters for all splicing events, we calculated the EF for a tissue at particular Ψ thresholds by using the population distribution of junction reads across individuals in the tissue. For each of four cutoff values c=1%, 5%, 10%, or 20%, we computed EF as the percentage of individuals with Ψ ≥ c from the CDF of the population distribution that was generated from the fitted model, and provide this value in a summary table (Supplementary Table 1). For a tissue with n individuals (almost always >100), we included events where the EF 5% was between 1% and 99%, excluding poorly spliced exons with EF below 1% and “canonical alternative” exons with EF > 99%.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, Jacobs et al. discuss naturally variable exons (NVEs) – exons that vary in splicing across individuals – by leveraging the large-scale tissue data made available by the GTEx project. The authors introduce a statistical approach that captures uncertainty in exon inclusion and estimate 56,415 NVEs. Further, the study defines exon frequency (EF) as a metric to describe the prevalence of NVEs in a population and demonstrate that most NVEs generally have low EFs and occur in coding regions. The authors characterize the functional importance of NVEs by assessing gene tolerance to LoF, as well as effects on gene expression and GWAS interpretation. They consider the contribution of both genetic and non-genetic variables to NVE presence. Moreover, the study tackles the challenging problem of variant interpretation and yields valuable insights by means of their logistic regression model SMS. Overall, the manuscript presents novel approaches to understanding splicing regulation at the individual level and I believe that this study would be a significant contribution to the field. Please see the questions below for further discussion.
1. How does the distribution of average total EJ reads per individual in Extended Data Fig. 1B compare to that of alternatively spliced non-NVEs. Also, please define top EF NVEs before mentioning for the first time in Extended Data Fig. 1B.
2. For highly covered splice junctions, an absolute log 10 ratio just under 1 could still represent a significant bias in coverage for the two splice junctions flanking a skipped exon. How was this threshold chosen, and could this introduce some noise downstream?
3. Given that exon skipping is generally more prevalent than alternative splice site usage, is the observed balance between the two types of splicing events expected among NVEs?
4. NVEs tend to occur at low frequencies. Is it be more appropriate to represent the default EF value of an NVE with a measure of central tendency (e.g. median) rather than the top EF across all tissues, which may be an outlier?
5. What is the exon length distribution of NVEs? Are high-frequency NVEs longer/shorter than low-frequency NVEs, and do they generally maintain/disrupt the reading frame?
6. For NVEalt_ss, 5’ and 3’ splice site motif scores are weaker than their cognates. Is this pattern similar or different for skipped exon NVEs?
7. Are there any similarities in biological pathways or functions among NVE-containing genes that share similar LEOUF scores?
8. The correlation shown in Extended Data Fig. 6 seems to be driven by splicing outliers. What is the correlation coefficient? Is it significant? Also, do the authors observe this correlation in the heart and blood?
9. In relation to the question above, can the authors provide support for their speculation of NMD being a potential mode of gene regulation by perhaps confirming the presence of a premature stop codon when the splicing of the ASGR1 NVE is altered?
10. Regarding the contribution of genetics to the presence of NVEs, do individuals that share an NVE also share similar genetic variants? What is the distribution of sQTLs (Fig. 5A) around and within the NVEs?
11. Most brain regions do not show virtually any correlation between age and NVEs. Interestingly, the substantia nigra has a relatively higher negative correlation. Can the authors comment or speculate on this pattern seen in the brain?
12. Page 22: “The variant alters predicted affinity for two of these RBPs (HNRNPK, PCBP1) by 5-fold and 4-fold, respectively, highlighting a potential molecular mechanism for this variant”. How were the RBP affinities quantified? Are these inferred from the SMS model or are they obtained from other external tools?
13. In relation to the previous question, do RBPs largely play a ubiquitous role in splicing of NVEs and non-NVEs (e.g. other AS exons), or do NVEs have stronger affinities for certain RBPs?
Minor comments:

Page 10: “The RNA-seq read depths available in GTEx are more than adequate to distinguish these moderate ψ values from absence of splicing, and NVEs possess splice site motifs very similar to those of other exons (Extended Data Fig. 2D), even for low-EF NVEs (Extended Data Fig. 2E).” Did the authors rather mean to reference Extended Data Figures 2E and 2F respectively?

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors make the interesting observation that a substantial number of exons and splice sites are used (i.e., spliced) in only a subset of individuals. They denote such events as NVEs. They show this formally using a beta-binomial model that learns a per tissue, cross-individual Beta prior on the PSI, which is used to both denoise the per individual estimates and better estimate the frequency of the NVE across individuals. They investigate various properties of these NVEs (sequence motifs) and the genes (conservation) they are found in, and relate them to know splicing QTLs. They show fine-mapped GWAS variants are somewhat enriched in NVEs (slightly more so than synonymous variants). By classifying NVEs as likely NMD-causing vs not, they find genetically regulated nmdNVEs tend to result in the expected effect on expression (as shown by eQTL data). Finally they develop a sQTL predictor, "SMS", which, when including NVE splice sites in its features, performs substantially better than spliceAI.
Overall, this is a interesting study with a number of interesting findings about interindividual variation in splicing in paricular and gene regulation in general. I have two major concerns.
1. The beta binomial model assumes a beta distribution for the underlying (unknown) distribution of true PSIs across individuals. As they mention, this is somewhat flexible but will not model all distributions. Even one of the examples shown in the manuscript (CAST, fig 1c) appears to be tri-modal with modes close to 0, 0.6, and 1, a distribution that a single beta will not be able to capture. Mixtures of Gaussians are known to be able to approximate any smooth distribution, so using a mixture of betas would be a tractable and flexible alternative to the single beta. By summing over the possible mixture assignments it is still possible to use LBFGS to fit this model. Given that the beta-binomial model is a key component of the analysis, I feel it should be ascertained whether the results are consistent using such an approach. It would additionally allow analysis of how often the distribution is unimodal/bi/trimodal etc.
2. The SMS part of the paper feels somewhat underdeveloped. There is no comparison to methods beyond SpliceAI (e.g. MTSplice or Pangolin), no mention of the sample size available for the logistic regression, and no assessment of which features are most important for the prediction. Unless I missed it it also wasn't specified whether an SMS is tissue specific or not? I'd almost be tempted to suggest cutting it, but the bump in AUPRC adding the NVE SSs is remarkable and would be a shame to miss.
It's not a major concern but the finding that NVEs are _more_ common in constrained genes warrants more discussion. Are the constrained genes more highly expressed making NVEs easily to detect? It might be worthwhile to ask if the NVE exons with highly constrained themselves are constrained as a class, compared to constitutive or canonical alternative exons (since testing individual exons would be underpowered).
Minor comments:
- "This exon appears completely absent or very lowly included in most people, but occurs at a Ψ of 5-10% in about 10% of individuals, with credible intervals on Ψ well separated from zero". This phrasing gives the impression there is bimodality, whereas really the data looks like a continuum to me.
- "This splicing variation does occur against" cut "does"
- Some amount of inter-individual variation in splicing for events differentially spliced between cell-types could be due to variable cell-type proportions. Cell type proportion estimates could be used to control for this possibility.
- the legend in 2b is confusing.
- several of the comparisons in "Most NVEs occur in coding regions and have low EF" would benefit from comparisons to a control set of exons.
- label 3a&b with which direction is more constrained
- what's going on with substantia nigra in 5b??
- psi_NVE should be labeled differently in eqns 1 and 2 since one is an estimate and one is a parameter
- "Where (cid:1) can be described as the prior"... alpha is a prior pseudocount, not a prior.
- "...using the L-BFGS-B algorithm (see Supplementary Note), using a beta prior with parameters α = β = 1" not sure what this means.
- "keeping one of the two inclusion introns to simplify the analysis" this is throwing out a lot of data. I think you could just take the average - the binomial likelihood in practice works fine for non integers.
- " we computed EF as the percentage of individuals with Ψ ≥ c from the modeled CDF of the population" assuming the CDF means the CDF of the fit beta(alpha,beta) (which should be clarified) then this implies getting the distribution correct is v important for defining NVEs, and further motivates the mixture of betas direction
- "90% of above" -> or
- "sQTL that we also eQTLs"
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Jacobs et al. characterize inter-individual variation on splicing using the GTEx dataset and report many “naturally variable exons” unannotated in GENCODE. Jacobs et al. analyzes transcriptomes from the GTEx project to identify exons that are present in some individuals but completely absent in others that the authors call “naturally variable exons” (NVEs). The authors show that NVEs are frequently missing from reference annotations (gencode) and that they are more common in genes that are less prone to loss-of-function mutations. Many NVEs are influenced by genetic variants and could help interpret causal genetic variants.
Overall, we find this work relevant as it reveals studies splicing variation in humans from a different perspective and offers significant implications for genetic research. We have some concerns/suggestions that we would like the authors to consider.
Major comments:
Some of the conclusions are not driven by statistically significant results, only by trends in the data, most likely due to power issues. However, these conclusions should be toned down and statistics should be added to some plots. In particular:
In Figure 2B (page 10) the authors mention: “NVEs with low EF are predominantly unannotated, while around half of high-EF NVEs are annotated”. However, in the plot the proportions do not seem different, all bars seem to be around 60%. The text could be improved by adding the exact percentages in the text or in the plotting area instead and if the percentages are not different enough, tone down the message of finding differences between low EF and high EF NVEs.
The authors report a correlation for Extended Data Fig. 6. However, a correlation coefficient, and a p-value (independently of it being significant or not) should be added to the plot to help readers interpret the correlation.
In Figure 3c, authors should explain what they refer to as “Enrichment”, similar to the explanation in the supplementary figure. Importantly, they report “The observed enrichments of causal variants in NVEs are above the level of synonymous variants, particularly at high PIP values, but below those of missense annotations”. According to the figure, the trend is not “particularly” but “only” observed at high PIP values, and the confidence intervals completely overlap, so it is not a significant result. The authors should tone down the results and state that “tend to be above” instead of “are above”. Furthermore, the sentence “Unannotated splicing events are enriched above synonymous at high PIPs” should be removed from the figure captions.
Figure 6A would benefit from having the (AUPRC) of the three curves, especially to support the claim: “When given access only to reference gene annotations, where the distance feature uses GENCODE splice sites (SMS-GENCODE), the method’s performance improves moderately over SpliceAI”. If not on the plot, the AUPRC should be stated in the text.
The Analysis shown in figure 5B should be redone, correcting for batch effects to confirm for age being the main explanatory factor for more NVEs. Batch effects such as ischemic time and hardy scale are a very important source of variation in the GTEx dataset.
In the first section of the results, the authors need to describe the methodology / cutoffs of actually calling NVEs in greater detail so that readers do not have to read the methods text to get a general idea of what cutoffs were used.
In the introduction, the authors mention evolution of new exons and draw some connections to why NVEs might represent evolutionarily new exons. This connection could be explored by examining sequence conservation characteristics of NVEs, likely as part of the “Most NVEs occur in coding regions and have low EF” section.
In the sentence “NVEs rarely occur in 3' UTRs, likely because they contain very few introns relative to other transcript regions”, the authors should elaborate to mention NMD, as this is the reason that 3’ UTRs do not contain introns.
In the sentence “Such a pattern could occur if NVEs arise more commonly in more constrained genes but often experience selection favoring lower ψ values, driving EFs lower, although other scenarios are possible”, the authors should elaborate on other scenarios. To me, what they propose seems possible but as it is the only scenario presented it is hard to assess. In connection with this, I think the hypothesis that the authors present is really interesting, but it would be strengthened through complementary analyses. For instance, the authors could examine the distribution of the metrics used to call NVEs of exons stratified by high or low LOEUF genes. Maybe this isn’t the best way to get an answer but it is what I can think of.
Regarding the analysis of the relationship of age versus number of NVEs, it would be interesting to see if the effect of age on NVEs could be correlated to the somatic mutation rate in the different GTEx tissues (https://doi.org/10.1186/s13073-020-00746-1) with the hypothesis being that the greater the mutation rate, the more variable splicing will be due to the genetic effects of somatic mutations.
Minor comments:
Supplementary Figure 5E figure caption is missing.
Authors should be consistent in the naming of the supplementary note figures. Sometimes they are referred to as “Supplementary Fig. 3” and sometimes as “Supplementary Note Fig. 5”.
Sometimes the authors use “an NVE” and some other “a NVE”. For example: “that describes the frequency of splicing of an NVE in a population, somewhat analogous to allele frequency (AF). The EF of a NVE…” in page 5.
Mention what NMD stands for the first time you mention it
The title of method section “sQTL that we also eQTLs” is unclear
References are missing in the paragraph: “The identification of variants that impact splicing remains challenging…” in page 18
In page 21: “When training on the top splicing signal (top PIP), i.e. the best splicing association for each unique variant, we obtained qualitatively similar results and the same ranking of algorithms (data not shown)”. Even if the data is not shown, the (AUPRC) could be reported in the text.
Regarding the statement “recent studies suggest that many exons are missing from transcriptome reference annotations, occurring only in a subset of transcriptomic datasets11,14,15 “. I don’t think GTEx is the paper for this statement.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Most mammalian genes undergo alternative splicing. The splicing of some exons has been acquired or lost in specific mammalian lineages, but differences in splicing within the human population are poorly understood. Using GTEx tissue transcriptomes from 838 individuals, we identified 57,271 “naturally variable exons” (NVEs) – exons which are included in mRNAs in some individuals but entirely excluded from others (or vice versa). NVEs impact three quarters of protein-coding genes, occur at all population frequencies, and are often absent from reference annotations. NVEs are more abundant in genes depleted of genetic loss-of-function mutations and aid in the interpretation of causal genetic variants. Genetic variants modulate the splicing of many NVEs, and 5’ untranslated region and coding-region NVEs are often associated with increased and decreased gene expression, respectively. Together, our findings characterize abundant splicing variation in the human population, with implications for a range of human genetic analyses.

---

## Introduction

Nearly all human genes undergo alternative splicing, in which distinct mRNAs derived from different combinations of exons and splice sites are produced from the same gene1. Small changes in mRNA sequence can exert large effects, including the addition/deletion of protein domains2,3, or production of functional versus nonfunctional isoforms, and dysregulation of splicing contributes to human disease4,5. Understanding variation in alternative splicing is therefore important in understanding physiological and disease mechanisms.

Evolutionarily conserved alternative exons tend to preserve protein reading frame6, and often exhibit tissue-specific regulation7. In addition, comparison across mammalian species has identified thousands of cases of complete loss or gain of the splicing of exons8, with more recently evolved exons more likely to occur in 5’ UTRs, where they are often associated with increased gene expression8. Gain or loss of the splicing of an exon in the coding sequence (CDS) may also influence expression by changing the reading frame, often triggering nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD)9,10. However, the evolution of alternative splicing within the human species remains poorly understood.

Most alternative exons are generally assumed to be spliced in all individuals, perhaps with different inclusion levels, a pattern which we call ‘canonical’ alternative splicing. Some such splicing differences are driven by genetic variation. Large-scale genetic association studies have associated changes in the usage of many alternatively spliced exons with single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), designated splicing quantitative trait loci (sQTLs)11,12. However, these variants typically have modest effect sizes, and their molecular mechanisms are often unclear. Ultra-rare genetic variants can sometimes lead to inclusion of previously unseen, “cryptic” exons or splice sites13. Some recent studies suggest that many exons are missing from transcriptome reference annotations, occurring only in a subset of transcriptomic datasets11,14,15. The availability of tissue transcriptomes from nearly 1000 individuals in the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project presents an opportunity to characterize human variation at the exon level, asking how often the presence/absence of individual exons or splice sites varies between the transcriptomes of different individuals.

One key challenge in the study of unannotated transcripts is assessing which reflect technical artifacts or other types of noise16,17, which are reproducible, and which have phenotypic effects18. A cross-species analysis has suggested that many unannotated splicing events in longer-lived organisms may represent “transcript drift”, and are often nonfunctional until they begin to splice in at higher levels19. However, another recent study found that lowly used exons that trigger NMD broadly impact gene expression in human lymphoblastoid cell lines, and can help interpret complex trait loci10.

Here, we define “naturally variable exons” (NVEs) as exons whose splicing is variable within the human population (i.e., not present in every individual), focusing on alternative “skipped” or “cassette” exons, and alternative splice sites, which extend or truncate exons. We introduce a statistical approach that estimates the population frequency with which NVEs are meaningfully included (at levels above 5%) in a human cohort, generating a quantitative atlas of splicing variation across tissues. Using data from GTEx, we find that NVEs impact most human genes, are sometimes associated with changes in gene expression, and can aid in the interpretation of non-coding genetic variants.

---

## Results

Generating a catalog of human NVEs
In order to generate a catalog of high-quality NVEs, we obtained mapped RNA-seq reads from 14,000 GTEx samples representing 49 tissues from 838 individuals11. To perform quality control and ensure accurate estimates of NVEs in the dataset, we devised a straightforward Bayesian approach. The method de-noises estimates by sharing signals across samples and enables estimation of the uncertainty in exon usage of each NVE.

To illustrate the method, consider an NVE of the alternative splice site variety, used in some individuals as an alternative to a canonical or “cognate” splice site, used in all people. The proportional use of the NVE within an individual – the “percent spliced in” (PSI or Ψ) – can be estimated from the proportion of RNA-seq reads that span the NVE and cognate exon junctions (EJs) (Supplementary Fig. 1A)20. NVEs tend to have fewer total junction reads per sample, making some estimates of Ψ less certain (Supplementary Fig. 1B). We therefore de-noised these estimates using a beta-binomial model, employing a mixture of 3 beta distributions for reasons discussed below. The workflow is described in Supplementary Fig. 1C, Methods and Supplementary Note Sections A-D. The method fits a smooth function representing the NVE’s underlying Ψ distribution across the population from the observed splice junction reads for an NVE across individuals in a tissue. We chose a mixture of 3 betas model because of its flexibility to model many different distributions and because many NVEs are associated with sQTLs (see below), which have 3 possible genotypes that may each generate distinct levels of splicing. The mixture of betas model can be used to assess uncertainty in Ψ values, and to estimate the proportion of individuals that splice the NVE at any given level. Here, we defined NVEs as alternative exons or splice sites that have estimated Ψ values of at least 5% in between 1% and 99% of the population in a particular tissue (see “Methods”); exons with Ψ ≥ 5% in over 99% of individuals are considered canonical alternative exons, and exons that don’t meet either of these criteria may be considered rare or cryptic exons. Using this definition, we identified 414,141 NVE-tissue pairs across all 49 tissues in the GTEx dataset (Supplementary Data 1), representing 57,271 unique NVEs. Like canonical alternative exons, NVEs are roughly balanced between the alternative splice site and skipped exon types (Supplementary Data 2).

Using these data, we define an interpretable summary statistic, exon frequency (EF), that describes the frequency of splicing of an NVE in a population, somewhat analogous to allele frequency (AF). The EF of an NVE in a tissue is the estimated proportion of individuals that splice the NVE at a threshold Ψ level or above. We typically employ a 5% Ψ threshold here because previous studies have suggested that this level of inclusion is near the lowest level where sequence conservation is commonly observed19. Distributions of EF values using different Ψ cutoffs are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1D

---

## Methods

Ethics statement
No primary data were generated for this study. Person-related data were obtained through authorized access from primary data controllers.

Datasets
GTEx release v8. From the GTEx download data portal, we downloaded splicing “phenotype” files, which were originally used as inputs of the original sQTL study in GTEx (v8 phg38). We accessed it using the GTEx data browser, and you can also use the requester pay google cloud bucket (gs://gtex-resources/GTEx_Analysis_v8_QTLs). Protected data, such as genotypes and metadata, were accessed via dbGaP (study accession: phs000424.v8.p2).

GTEx fine-mapped sQTLs and eQTLs. Baberia et al. fine-mapped sQTLs and eQTLS in GTEx using the DAP-G fine-mapping method. We accessed this dataset using their Zenodo link. Note that fine-mapping was performed only on European ancestry samples from GTEx.

gnomAD. We accessed LOEUF scores from gnomAD v4.0 using the gnomAD data browser (linked here), which computed the LOEUF across nearly all genes in the genome.

GENCODE exon annotations. We accessed comprehensive transcript annotations from GENCODE v44 using their data browser, for use as our reference set of exons.

SpliceAI scores. SpliceAI scores have been computed across the genome (all possible SNP mutations). To compare the differences in SMS and spliceAI scores, we used a dataset that released all variants with SpliceAI scores above a nominal threshold (>0.1), which are available in the Illumina data browser (link: https://basespace.illumina.com/s/otSPW8hnhaZR). All other variants were set to 0.

Fine-mapped BioBank (GWAS) data
UKBB (96 traits): https://github.com/mkanai/finemapping-insights, including ASGR1 exon 4
Biobank Japan: https://pheweb.jp/downloads
FinnGen: https://www.finngen.fi/en/researchers/data_available

Data preprocessing
GTEx LeafCutter phenotypes. LeafCutter intron clusters were required to include only 2 or 3 introns, so we could classify them as alternative 3’ or 5’ splice sites or skipped exons, respectively. We mapped to genes and strands by scoring every splice site in the cluster, and picking the strand that had MaxEnt scores > 0 for all splice sites, excluding any clusters that did not score above zero across all splice sites on either strand as potential artefacts. Only protein-coding genes were included. Lastly, exons were required to be ≤ 500 bp in length and alternative splice sites were required to be within 500 bp of each other.

Generating estimates of Ψ values of NVEs
Many NVEs have fairly low inclusion levels, so to estimate their usage accurately, we built a model to assess their abundance in an RNA-sequencing sample. We considered a potential NVE in relation to a more frequently observed “cognate” junction in transcripts from the same gene.

PSI (Ψ) estimates the fraction of a gene’s transcripts that contain the exon or splice site of interest and is a widely used statistic to quantify splicing. It can be estimated from any RNA-seq dataset with sufficient read coverage of the alternative region:

ψ NVE = EJ reads NVE / (EJ reads NVE + EJ reads cognate)

We consider the exon or splice junction with fewer reads across all individuals a candidate NVE, and the exon or splice junction with more reads as the cognate.

Conditional on Ψ, the number of NVE reads in an RNA-seq dataset can be modeled as a binomial distribution, as defined by LeafCutter splicing33 clusters:

NVE reads | ψ ~ Binomial(EJ reads NVE + EJ reads cognate, Ψ NVE)

Note that we have to frame the exon junction reads slightly differently in alternative splice sites as compared to skipped exons to model the NVE (Supp. Fig. 1A).

Mixture of Betas binomial model
Partial pooling involves using information across samples to estimate effect sizes of individual samples by fitting a population distribution to the observed data and letting that inform effect size estimates for individuals54,55.

For proof of concept, the NVE population distribution can be modeled with a single beta distribution with parameters α and β:

ψ NVE ~ Beta(α, β)

Where α can be described as the pseudocount on the splicing of the NVEs splicing event, and β can be described as the pseudocount on the splicing of the cognate splicing event, respectively. In other words, in the absence of read count data, α and β provide an initial estimate of the splicing of the NVE.

A single beta distribution can capture several common situations (but not all – see Supplementary Note). One example of a distribution that a single beta cannot handle is a trimodal distribution, which would be expected for an NVE whose splicing differs between three subsets of the population. Because trimodal distributions are interesting biologically, potentially representing cases where a single variant (that may be absent or present in heterozygous or homozygous form) drives the inclusion of an NVE, we decided to fit a three-component mixture of betas model to all exons in the dataset. We compare this result to a single beta model in the Supplementary Note Sections E-F, and find that the summary statistic, EF, is fairly robust in both three- and one-component models.

For a three-component beta distribution, with parameters α and β, the NVE population distribution can be modeled with nine parameters:

ψ NVE ~ Σ i=1 to 3 γ i Beta(α i, β i)

Where γ i are weights that represent the fraction of the distribution coming from each individual beta distribution, requiring that all γ i ≥ 0, and that they sum to 1. Note that the triple-beta distribution can model a two-beta or single beta distribution by setting one or two of the γ parameters to zero. We can then estimate the population distribution of a given tissue sample:

PDF NVE = Σ i=1 to 3 γ i * PDF Beta(α i, β i)

The task is to predict the population distribution of a splicing event in a given tissue sample. We employ maximum likelihood estimation with the expectation maximization algorithm. The algorithm is initialized with uniform weights, α=(1,2,3), and β=(3,2,1) as an unbiased starting point able to capture symmetric and asymmetric distributions. It then iteratively performs the E-step to analytically find optimal weights γ, and the M-step to determine the α, β using the L-BFGS-B optimization algorithm. The method is represented graphically in Fig. 1A.

Alternative splice site NVEs
We searched for the optimal α, β, and γ parameters that best fit the data, using the expectation maximization framework (see Supplementary Note Sections B-C).

Skipped exon NVEs
Skipped exons are represented by three intron clusters: two introns supporting the inclusion of the exon, and one longer intron excluding the exon. We include events where both inclusion introns have numbers of reads that are not drastically different (see Supplementary Fig. 11), keeping one of the two inclusion introns to simplify the analysis. We then followed the same approach as for alternative splice sites to find the optimal parameters.

Calculation of exon frequency (EF) at a given Ψ threshold
We estimated the Ψ of all NVEs of length ≤ 500 (for skipped exons) or inter-splice site distance ≤ 500 bp (see Supp. Fig. 16), as this size capture the vast majority (>99%) of known internal exons and alternative splice sites in the human transcriptome. After obtaining the population parameters for all splicing events, we calculated the EF for a tissue at particular Ψ thresholds by using the population distribution of junction reads across individuals in the tissue. For each of four cutoff values c=1%, 5%, 10%, or 20%, we computed EF as the percentage of individuals with Ψ ≥ c from the CDF of the population distribution that was generated from the fitted model, and provide this value in a summary table (Supplementary Table 1). For a tissue with n individuals (almost always >100), we included events where the EF 5% was between 1% and 99%, excluding poorly spliced exons with EF below 1% and “canonical alternative” exons with EF > 99%.

Following ref. 56, to obtain an estimated Ψ value for an NVE in a single individual, we computed the mean posterior on Ψ and standard deviation of the estimate in each individual in the tissue by using the α and β parameters estimated from the 3-beta mixture binomial fit described above. Further, the study defines exon frequency (EF) as a metric to describe the prevalence of NVEs in a population and demonstrate that most NVEs generally have low EFs and occur in coding regions. The authors characterize the functional importance of NVEs by assessing gene tolerance to LoF, as well as effects on gene expression and GWAS interpretation. They consider the contribution of both genetic and non-genetic variables to NVE presence. Moreover, the study tackles the challenging problem of variant interpretation and yields valuable insights by means of their logistic regression model SMS. Overall, the manuscript presents novel approaches to understanding splicing regulation at the individual level and I believe that this study would be a significant contribution to the field. Please see the questions below for further discussion.
1. How does the distribution of average total EJ reads per individual in Extended Data Fig. 1B compare to that of alternatively spliced non-NVEs. Also, please define top EF NVEs before mentioning for the first time in Extended Data Fig. 1B.
2. For highly covered splice junctions, an absolute log 10 ratio just under 1 could still represent a significant bias in coverage for the two splice junctions flanking a skipped exon. How was this threshold chosen, and could this introduce some noise downstream?
3. Given that exon skipping is generally more prevalent than alternative splice site usage, is the observed balance between the two types of splicing events expected among NVEs?
4. NVEs tend to occur at low frequencies. Is it be more appropriate to represent the default EF value of an NVE with a measure of central tendency (e.g. median) rather than the top EF across all tissues, which may be an outlier?
5. What is the exon length distribution of NVEs? Are high-frequency NVEs longer/shorter than low-frequency NVEs, and do they generally maintain/disrupt the reading frame?
6. For NVEalt_ss, 5’ and 3’ splice site motif scores are weaker than their cognates. Is this pattern similar or different for skipped exon NVEs?
7. Are there any similarities in biological pathways or functions among NVE-containing genes that share similar LEOUF scores?
8. The correlation shown in Extended Data Fig. 6 seems to be driven by splicing outliers. What is the correlation coefficient? Is it significant? Also, do the authors observe this correlation in the heart and blood?
9. In relation to the question above, can the authors provide support for their speculation of NMD being a potential mode of gene regulation by perhaps confirming the presence of a premature stop codon when the splicing of the ASGR1 NVE is altered?
10. Regarding the contribution of genetics to the presence of NVEs, do individuals that share an NVE also share similar genetic variants? What is the distribution of sQTLs (Fig. 5A) around and within the NVEs?
11. Most brain regions do not show virtually any correlation between age and NVEs. Interestingly, the substantia nigra has a relatively higher negative correlation. Can the authors comment or speculate on this pattern seen in the brain?
12. Page 22: “The variant alters predicted affinity for two of these RBPs (HNRNPK, PCBP1) by 5-fold and 4-fold, respectively, highlighting a potential molecular mechanism for this variant”. How were the RBP affinities quantified? Are these inferred from the SMS model or are they obtained from other external tools?
13. In relation to the previous question, do RBPs largely play a ubiquitous role in splicing of NVEs and non-NVEs (e.g. other AS exons), or do NVEs have stronger affinities for certain RBPs?

### Reviewer 2

The authors make the interesting observation that a substantial number of exons and splice sites are used (i.e., spliced) in only a subset of individuals. They denote such events as NVEs. They show this formally using a beta-binomial model that learns a per tissue, cross-individual Beta prior on the PSI, which is used to both denoise the per individual estimates and better estimate the frequency of the NVE across individuals. They investigate various properties of these NVEs (sequence motifs) and the genes (conservation) they are found in, and relate them to know splicing QTLs. They show fine-mapped GWAS variants are somewhat enriched in NVEs (slightly more so than synonymous variants). By classifying NVEs as likely NMD-causing vs not, they find genetically regulated nmdNVEs tend to result in the expected effect on expression (as shown by eQTL data). Finally they develop a sQTL predictor, "SMS", which, when including NVE splice sites in its features, performs substantially better than spliceAI.

1. The beta binomial model assumes a beta distribution for the underlying (unknown) distribution of true PSIs across individuals. As they mention, this is somewhat flexible but will not model all distributions. Even one of the examples shown in the manuscript (CAST, fig 1c) appears to be tri-modal with modes close to 0, 0.6, and 1, a distribution that a single beta will not be able to capture. Mixtures of Gaussians are known to be able to approximate any smooth distribution, so using a mixture of betas would be a tractable and flexible alternative to the single beta. By summing over the possible mixture assignments it is still possible to use LBFGS to fit this model. Given that the beta-binomial model is a key component of the analysis, I feel it should be ascertained whether the results are consistent using such an approach. It would additionally allow analysis of how often the distribution is unimodal/bi/trimodal etc.
2. The SMS part of the paper feels somewhat underdeveloped. There is no comparison to methods beyond SpliceAI (e.g. MTSplice or Pangolin), no mention of the sample size available for the logistic regression, and no assessment of which features are most important for the prediction. - "sQTL that we also eQTLs"

### Reviewer 3

Jacobs et al. characterize inter-individual variation on splicing using the GTEx dataset and report many “naturally variable exons” unannotated in GENCODE. Jacobs et al. analyzes transcriptomes from the GTEx project to identify exons that are present in some individuals but completely absent in others that the authors call “naturally variable exons” (NVEs). The authors show that NVEs are frequently missing from reference annotations (gencode) and that they are more common in genes that are less prone to loss-of-function mutations. Many NVEs are influenced by genetic variants and could help interpret causal genetic variants.
Overall, we find this work relevant as it reveals studies splicing variation in humans from a different perspective and offers significant implications for genetic research. We have some concerns/suggestions that we would like the authors to consider.
Major comments:
Some of the conclusions are not driven by statistically significant results, only by trends in the data, most likely due to power issues. However, these conclusions should be toned down and statistics should be added to some plots. In particular:
In Figure 2B (page 10) the authors mention: “NVEs with low EF are predominantly unannotated, while around half of high-EF NVEs are annotated”. ## Paper

## Abstract

Most mammalian genes undergo alternative splicing. The splicing of some exons has been acquired or lost in specific mammalian lineages, but differences in splicing within the human population are poorly understood. Using GTEx tissue transcriptomes from 838 individuals, we identified 57,271 “naturally variable exons” (NVEs) – exons which are included in mRNAs in some individuals but entirely excluded from others (or vice versa). NVEs impact three quarters of protein-coding genes, occur at all population frequencies, and are often absent from reference annotations. NVEs are more abundant in genes depleted of genetic loss-of-function mutations and aid in the interpretation of causal genetic variants. Genetic variants modulate the splicing of many NVEs, and 5’ untranslated region and coding-region NVEs are often associated with increased and decreased gene expression, respectively. Together, our findings characterize abundant splicing variation in the human population, with implications for a range of human genetic analyses.

---

## Introduction

Nearly all human genes undergo alternative splicing, in which distinct mRNAs derived from different combinations of exons and splice sites are produced from the same gene1. Small changes in mRNA sequence can exert large effects, including the addition/deletion of protein domains2,3, or production of functional versus nonfunctional isoforms, and dysregulation of splicing contributes to human disease4,5. Understanding variation in alternative splicing is therefore important in understanding physiological and disease mechanisms.

Evolutionarily conserved alternative exons tend to preserve protein reading frame6, and often exhibit tissue-specific regulation7. In addition, comparison across mammalian species has identified thousands of cases of complete loss or gain of the splicing of exons8, with more recently evolved exons more likely to occur in 5’ UTRs, where they are often associated with increased gene expression8. Gain or loss of the splicing of an exon in the coding sequence (CDS) may also influence expression by changing the reading frame, often triggering nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD)9,10. However, the evolution of alternative splicing within the human species remains poorly understood.

Most alternative exons are generally assumed to be spliced in all individuals, perhaps with different inclusion levels, a pattern which we call ‘canonical’ alternative splicing. Some such splicing differences are driven by genetic variation. Large-scale genetic association studies have associated changes in the usage of many alternatively spliced exons with single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), designated splicing quantitative trait loci (sQTLs)11,12. However, these variants typically have modest effect sizes, and their molecular mechanisms are often unclear. Ultra-rare genetic variants can sometimes lead to inclusion of previously unseen, “cryptic” exons or splice sites13. Some recent studies suggest that many exons are missing from transcriptome reference annotations, occurring only in a subset of transcriptomic datasets11,14,15. The availability of tissue transcriptomes from nearly 1000 individuals in the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project presents an opportunity to characterize human variation at the exon level, asking how often the presence/absence of individual exons or splice sites varies between the transcriptomes of different individuals.

One key challenge in the study of unannotated transcripts is assessing which reflect technical artifacts or other types of noise16,17, which are reproducible, and which have phenotypic effects18. A cross-species analysis has suggested that many unannotated splicing events in longer-lived organisms may represent “transcript drift”, and are often nonfunctional until they begin to splice in at higher levels19. However, another recent study found that lowly used exons that trigger NMD broadly impact gene expression in human lymphoblastoid cell lines, and can help interpret complex trait loci10.

Here, we define “naturally variable exons” (NVEs) as exons whose splicing is variable within the human population (i.e., not present in every individual), focusing on alternative “skipped” or “cassette” exons, and alternative splice sites, which extend or truncate exons. We introduce a statistical approach that estimates the population frequency with which NVEs are meaningfully included (at levels above 5%) in a human cohort, generating a quantitative atlas of splicing variation across tissues. Using data from GTEx, we find that NVEs impact most human genes, are sometimes associated with changes in gene expression, and can aid in the interpretation of non-coding genetic variants.

---

## Results

Generating a catalog of human NVEs
In order to generate a catalog of high-quality NVEs, we obtained mapped RNA-seq reads from 14,000 GTEx samples representing 49 tissues from 838 individuals11. To perform quality control and ensure accurate estimates of NVEs in the dataset, we devised a straightforward Bayesian approach. The method de-noises estimates by sharing signals across samples and enables estimation of the uncertainty in exon usage of each NVE.

To illustrate the method, consider an NVE of the alternative splice site variety, used in some individuals as an alternative to a canonical or “cognate” splice site, used in all people. The proportional use of the NVE within an individual – the “percent spliced in” (PSI or Ψ) – can be estimated from the proportion of RNA-seq reads that span the NVE and cognate exon junctions (EJs) (Supplementary Fig. 1A)20. NVEs tend to have fewer total junction reads per sample, making some estimates of Ψ less certain (Supplementary Fig. 1B). We therefore de-noised these estimates using a beta-binomial model, employing a mixture of 3 beta distributions for reasons discussed below. The workflow is described in Supplementary Fig. 1C, Methods and Supplementary Note Sections A-D. The method fits a smooth function representing the NVE’s underlying Ψ distribution across the population from the observed splice junction reads for an NVE across individuals in a tissue. We chose a mixture of 3 betas model because of its flexibility to model many different distributions and because many NVEs are associated with sQTLs (see below), which have 3 possible genotypes that may each generate distinct levels of splicing. The mixture of betas model can be used to assess uncertainty in Ψ values, and to estimate the proportion of individuals that splice the NVE at any given level. Here, we defined NVEs as alternative exons or splice sites that have estimated Ψ values of at least 5% in between 1% and 99% of the population in a particular tissue (see “Methods”); exons with Ψ ≥ 5% in over 99% of individuals are considered canonical alternative exons, and exons that don’t meet either of these criteria may be considered rare or cryptic exons. Using this definition, we identified 414,141 NVE-tissue pairs across all 49 tissues in the GTEx dataset (Supplementary Data 1), representing 57,271 unique NVEs. Like canonical alternative exons, NVEs are roughly balanced between the alternative splice site and skipped exon types (Supplementary Data 2).

Using these data, we define an interpretable summary statistic, exon frequency (EF), that describes the frequency of splicing of an NVE in a population, somewhat analogous to allele frequency (AF). The EF of an NVE in a tissue is the estimated proportion of individuals that splice the NVE at a threshold Ψ level or above. We typically employ a 5% Ψ threshold here because previous studies have suggested that this level of inclusion is near the lowest level where sequence conservation is commonly observed19. Distributions of EF values using different Ψ cutoffs are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1D

## Methods

Ethics statement
No primary data were generated for this study. Person-related data were obtained through authorized access from primary data controllers.

Datasets
GTEx release v8. From the GTEx download data portal, we downloaded splicing “phenotype” files, which were originally used as inputs of the original sQTL study in GTEx (v8 phg38). We accessed it using the GTEx data browser, and you can also use the requester pay google cloud bucket (gs://gtex-resources/GTEx_Analysis_v8_QTLs). Protected data, such as genotypes and metadata, were accessed via dbGaP (study accession: phs000424.v8.p2).

GTEx fine-mapped sQTLs and eQTLs. Baberia et al. fine-mapped sQTLs and eQTLS in GTEx using the DAP-G fine-mapping method. We accessed this dataset using their Zenodo link. Note that fine-mapping was performed only on European ancestry samples from GTEx.

gnomAD. We accessed LOEUF scores from gnomAD v4.0 using the gnomAD data browser (linked here), which computed the LOEUF across nearly all genes in the genome.

GENCODE exon annotations. We accessed comprehensive transcript annotations from GENCODE v44 using their data browser, for use as our reference set of exons.

SpliceAI scores. SpliceAI scores have been computed across the genome (all possible SNP mutations). To compare the differences in SMS and spliceAI scores, we used a dataset that released all variants with SpliceAI scores above a nominal threshold (>0.1), which are available in the Illumina data browser (link: https://basespace.illumina.com/s/otSPW8hnhaZR). All other variants were set to 0.

Fine-mapped BioBank (GWAS) data
UKBB (96 traits): https://github.com/mkanai/finemapping-insights, including ASGR1 exon 4
Biobank Japan: https://pheweb.jp/downloads
FinnGen: https://www.finngen.fi/en/researchers/data_available

Data preprocessing
GTEx LeafCutter phenotypes. LeafCutter intron clusters were required to include only 2 or 3 introns, so we could classify them as alternative 3’ or 5’ splice sites or skipped exons, respectively. We mapped to genes and strands by scoring every splice site in the cluster, and picking the strand that had MaxEnt scores > 0 for all splice sites, excluding any clusters that did not score above zero across all splice sites on either strand as potential artefacts. Only protein-coding genes were included. Lastly, exons were required to be ≤ 500 bp in length and alternative splice sites were required to be within 500 bp of each other.

Generating estimates of Ψ values of NVEs
Many NVEs have fairly low inclusion levels, so to estimate their usage accurately, we built a model to assess their abundance in an RNA-sequencing sample. We considered a potential NVE in relation to a more frequently observed “cognate” junction in transcripts from the same gene.

PSI (Ψ) estimates the fraction of a gene’s transcripts that contain the exon or splice site of interest and is a widely used statistic to quantify splicing. It can be estimated from any RNA-seq dataset with sufficient read coverage of the alternative region:

ψ NVE = EJ reads NVE / (EJ reads NVE + EJ reads cognate)

We consider the exon or splice junction with fewer reads across all individuals a candidate NVE, and the exon or splice junction with more reads as the cognate.

Conditional on Ψ, the number of NVE reads in an RNA-seq dataset can be modeled as a binomial distribution, as defined by LeafCutter splicing33 clusters:

NVE reads | ψ ~ Binomial(EJ reads NVE + EJ reads cognate, Ψ NVE)

Note that we have to frame the exon junction reads slightly differently in alternative splice sites as compared to skipped exons to model the NVE (Supp. Fig. 1A).

Mixture of Betas binomial model
Partial pooling involves using information across samples to estimate effect sizes of individual samples by fitting a population distribution to the observed data and letting that inform effect size estimates for individuals54,55.

For proof of concept, the NVE population distribution can be modeled with a single beta distribution with parameters α and β:

ψ NVE ~ Beta(α, β)

Where α can be described as the pseudocount on the splicing of the NVEs splicing event, and β can be described as the pseudocount on the splicing of the cognate splicing event, respectively. In other words, in the absence of read count data, α and β provide an initial estimate of the splicing of the NVE.

A single beta distribution can capture several common situations (but not all – see Supplementary Note). One example of a distribution that a single beta cannot handle is a trimodal distribution, which would be expected for an NVE whose splicing differs between three subsets of the population. Because trimodal distributions are interesting biologically, potentially representing cases where a single variant (that may be absent or present in heterozygous or homozygous form) drives the inclusion of an NVE, we decided to fit a three-component mixture of betas model to all exons in the dataset. We compare this result to a single beta model in the Supplementary Note Sections E-F, and find that the summary statistic, EF, is fairly robust in both three- and one-component models.

For a three-component beta distribution, with parameters α and β, the NVE population distribution can be modeled with nine parameters:

ψ NVE ~ Σ i=1 to 3 γ i Beta(α i, β i)

Where γ i are weights that represent the fraction of the distribution coming from each individual beta distribution, requiring that all γ i ≥ 0, and that they sum to 1. Note that the triple-beta distribution can model a two-beta or single beta distribution by setting one or two of the γ parameters to zero. We can then estimate the population distribution of a given tissue sample:

PDF NVE = Σ i=1 to 3 γ i * PDF Beta(α i, β i)

The task is to predict the population distribution of a splicing event in a given tissue sample. We employ maximum likelihood estimation with the expectation maximization algorithm. The algorithm is initialized with uniform weights, α=(1,2,3), and β=(3,2,1) as an unbiased starting point able to capture symmetric and asymmetric distributions. It then iteratively performs the E-step to analytically find optimal weights γ, and the M-step to determine the α, β using the L-BFGS-B optimization algorithm. The method is represented graphically in Fig. 1A.

Alternative splice site NVEs
We searched for the optimal α, β, and γ parameters that best fit the data, using the expectation maximization framework (see Supplementary Note Sections B-C).

Skipped exon NVEs
Skipped exons are represented by three intron clusters: two introns supporting the inclusion of the exon, and one longer intron excluding the exon. We include events where both inclusion introns have numbers of reads that are not drastically different (see Supplementary Fig. 11), keeping one of the two inclusion introns to simplify the analysis. We then followed the same approach as for alternative splice sites to find the optimal parameters.

Calculation of exon frequency (EF) at a given Ψ threshold
We estimated the Ψ of all NVEs of length ≤ 500 (for skipped exons) or inter-splice site distance ≤ 500 bp (see Supp. Fig. 16), as this size capture the vast majority (>99%) of known internal exons and alternative splice sites in the human transcriptome. After obtaining the population parameters for all splicing events, we calculated the EF for a tissue at particular Ψ thresholds by using the population distribution of junction reads across individuals in the tissue. For each of four cutoff values c=1%, 5%, 10%, or 20%, we computed EF as the percentage of individuals with Ψ ≥ c from the CDF of the population distribution that was generated from the fitted model, and provide this value in a summary table (Supplementary Table 1). For a tissue with n individuals (almost always >100), we included events where the EF 5% was between 1% and 99%, excluding poorly spliced exons with EF below 1% and “canonical alternative” exons with EF > 99%.

### Reviewer 2

The authors make the interesting observation that a substantial number of exons and splice sites are used (i.e., spliced) in only a subset of individuals. They denote such events as NVEs. They show this formally using a beta-binomial model that learns a per tissue, cross-individual Beta prior on the PSI, which is used to both denoise the per individual estimates and better estimate the frequency of the NVE across individuals. They investigate various properties of these NVEs (sequence motifs) and the genes (conservation) they are found in, and relate them to know splicing QTLs. They show fine-mapped GWAS variants are somewhat enriched in NVEs (slightly more so than synonymous variants). By classifying NVEs as likely NMD-causing vs not, they find genetically regulated nmdNVEs tend to result in the expected effect on expression (as shown by eQTL data). Finally they develop a sQTL predictor, "SMS", which, when including NVE splice sites in its features, performs substantially better than spliceAI.
Overall, this is a interesting study with a number of interesting findings about interindividual variation in splicing in paricular and gene regulation in general. I have two major concerns.
1. The beta binomial model assumes a beta distribution for the underlying (unknown) distribution of true PSIs across individuals. As they mention, this is somewhat flexible but will not model all distributions. Even one of the examples shown in the manuscript (CAST, fig 1c) appears to be tri-modal with modes close to 0, 0.6, and 1, a distribution that a single beta will not be able to capture. Mixtures of Gaussians are known to be able to approximate any smooth distribution, so using a mixture of betas would be a tractable and flexible alternative to the single beta. By summing over the possible mixture assignments it is still possible to use LBFGS to fit this model. Given that the beta-binomial model is a key component of the analysis, I feel it should be ascertained whether the results are consistent using such an approach. It would additionally allow analysis of how often the distribution is unimodal/bi/trimodal etc.
2. The SMS part of the paper feels somewhat underdeveloped. There is no comparison to methods beyond SpliceAI (e.g. MTSplice or Pangolin), no mention of the sample size available for the logistic regression, and no assessment of which features are most important for the prediction. Unless I missed it it also wasn't specified whether an SMS is tissue specific or not? I'd almost be tempted to suggest cutting it, but the bump in AUPRC adding the NVE SSs is remarkable and would be a shame to miss.
It's not a major concern but the finding that NVEs are _more_ common in constrained genes warrants more discussion. Are the constrained genes more highly expressed making NVEs easily to detect? It might be worthwhile to ask if the NVE exons with highly constrained themselves are constrained as a class, compared to constitutive or canonical alternative exons (since testing individual exons would be underpowered).

We implemented a 3-component mixture of betas model and applied it across all exons
in GTEx. Briefly, we use LBFGS and expectation maximization to approximate the most
likely parameters that can be described using a mixture of betas given the data. We
chose a 3-component model because of its flexibility to model many different
distributions and because of our finding that many NVEs are associated with sQTLs,
which have 3 possible genotypes that might each generate distinct splicing patterns.

and new mixture models give similar EFs for the NVEs reported previously (Reviewer

details, including simulations showing that a 3-component mixture model can handle
many different distributions of PSI values. The released code has also been updated so
that users can choose whether to use a 1-component, 2-component or 3-component
model to fit observed RNAseq data. The major difference between our results with a
single beta and those with the mixture model is that the resulting distribution of EFs is

## Paper

## Abstract

Most mammalian genes undergo alternative splicing. The splicing of some exons has been acquired or lost in specific mammalian lineages, but differences in splicing within the human population are poorly understood. Using GTEx tissue transcriptomes from 838 individuals, we identified 57,271 “naturally variable exons” (NVEs) – exons which are included in mRNAs in some individuals but entirely excluded from others (or vice versa). NVEs impact three quarters of protein-coding genes, occur at all population frequencies, and are often absent from reference annotations. NVEs are more abundant in genes depleted of genetic loss-of-function mutations and aid in the interpretation of causal genetic variants. Genetic variants modulate the splicing of many NVEs, and 5’ untranslated region and coding-region NVEs are often associated with increased and decreased gene expression, respectively. Together, our findings characterize abundant splicing variation in the human population, with implications for a range of human genetic analyses.

## Introduction

Nearly all human genes undergo alternative splicing, in which distinct mRNAs derived from different combinations of exons and splice sites are produced from the same gene1. Small changes in mRNA sequence can exert large effects, including the addition/deletion of protein domains2,3, or production of functional versus nonfunctional isoforms, and dysregulation of splicing contributes to human disease4,5. Understanding variation in alternative splicing is therefore important in understanding physiological and disease mechanisms.

Evolutionarily conserved alternative exons tend to preserve protein reading frame6, and often exhibit tissue-specific regulation7. In addition, comparison across mammalian species has identified thousands of cases of complete loss or gain of the splicing of exons8, with more recently evolved exons more likely to occur in 5’ UTRs, where they are often associated with increased gene expression8. Gain or loss of the splicing of an exon in the coding sequence (CDS) may also influence expression by changing the reading frame, often triggering nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD)9,10. However, the evolution of alternative splicing within the human species remains poorly understood.

Most alternative exons are generally assumed to be spliced in all individuals, perhaps with different inclusion levels, a pattern which we call ‘canonical’ alternative splicing. Some such splicing differences are driven by genetic variation. Large-scale genetic association studies have associated changes in the usage of many alternatively spliced exons with single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), designated splicing quantitative trait loci (sQTLs)11,12. However, these variants typically have modest effect sizes, and their molecular mechanisms are often unclear. Ultra-rare genetic variants can sometimes lead to inclusion of previously unseen, “cryptic” exons or splice sites13. Some recent studies suggest that many exons are missing from transcriptome reference annotations, occurring only in a subset of transcriptomic datasets11,14,15. The availability of tissue transcriptomes from nearly 1000 individuals in the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project presents an opportunity to characterize human variation at the exon level, asking how often the presence/absence of individual exons or splice sites varies between the transcriptomes of different individuals.

One key challenge in the study of unannotated transcripts is assessing which reflect technical artifacts or other types of noise16,17, which are reproducible, and which have phenotypic effects18. A cross-species analysis has suggested that many unannotated splicing events in longer-lived organisms may represent “transcript drift”, and are often nonfunctional until they begin to splice in at higher levels19. However, another recent study found that lowly used exons that trigger NMD broadly impact gene expression in human lymphoblastoid cell lines, and can help interpret complex trait loci10.

Here, we define “naturally variable exons” (NVEs) as exons whose splicing is variable within the human population (i.e., not present in every individual), focusing on alternative “skipped” or “cassette” exons, and alternative splice sites, which extend or truncate exons. We introduce a statistical approach that estimates the population frequency with which NVEs are meaningfully included (at levels above 5%) in a human cohort, generating a quantitative atlas of splicing variation across tissues. Using data from GTEx, we find that NVEs impact most human genes, are sometimes associated with changes in gene expression, and can aid in the interpretation of non-coding genetic variants.
